# Build a Reusable Alexa+ Morning Routine That Runs the Same Way Every Weekday

> **In short:** Yes — one Alexa+ routine can do news, weather, calendar and lights from a single voice phrase. App layouts vary by version, so this guide points to where things usually live rather than naming buttons we haven't seen.

By the end of this guide, you'll have one spoken phrase that does four things in a row every weekday morning, without picking up your phone. This is for people who already use Alexa+ for the basics (asking questions, setting timers) and want to make the morning automatic.

## Before you start
- An **Amazon account** linked to your Alexa device, with the **Alexa app** installed on your phone.
- A working **Alexa+ setup**. Depending on your plan and region, some routine features may sit behind a paid Alexa+ tier — check Amazon's current offering if you're unsure.
- About **15 minutes** for the first build, plus a quick test.
- Optional but useful: a smart light already named in the Alexa app (e.g., "Bedroom Lamp") and a calendar (Google, Outlook or Apple) already linked inside Alexa. Routines can only call on features that are already connected.

## Step 1 — Decide what your morning routine should include
Open a notes app — or grab a piece of paper — and write down the four or five things you want Alexa to do, in the order you want them to happen. A reusable routine is just a saved list of actions, so the clearer your list, the faster the rest of this build goes.

For a typical weekday, a useful starter set is: a short news briefing, today's weather, your first few calendar events, and turning on one smart light. You can always add or remove actions later — but starting with a written list keeps every later step short.

💬 Example:
**News flash → Weather for my location → Read today's calendar → Turn on Bedroom Lamp**

If you'd rather plan by speaking, you can dictate the same list into a voice memo — the format doesn't matter, only the order does.

**You'll know it worked when** you have a written (or typed, or recorded) list of 3–6 actions, each starting with a verb like "play", "read", "turn on" or "tell me".

## Step 2 — Open the Alexa app and find the Routines section
Open the Alexa app on your phone and look for a menu option labeled something like **Routines** — it's usually inside a "More" tab, a "Settings" area, or directly on the home screen. If you can't find it, try the in-app **search bar** with the word "routine"; the app's layout has changed several times, and Amazon has shipped new designs alongside Alexa+, so the exact path differs.

When you find it, tap the option to **create a new routine**. A mostly blank routine editor should open, usually with sections for a name, a trigger (what starts the routine) and a list of actions (what the routine does).

If your app shows "Alexa+ Routines", "AI Routines" or anything similar instead of plain "Routines", that's fine — pick whichever routine creator is available; the workflow is similar across them.

💬 Example: a routine name
**Weekday Morning**

**You'll know it worked when** you can see an empty routine with fields for a trigger and at least one action.

## Step 3 — Set the trigger to a voice phrase you'll actually say
A trigger is what starts the routine — a spoken phrase, a specific time, or both. For a hands-free morning, the most useful trigger is a short **voice phrase** you say out loud. Look for a trigger option called something like "When you say", "Voice" or "Phrase", then type in the words you want.

Pick something short, distinctive, and unlikely to come up in normal conversation — avoid phrases like "good morning" on their own, because Alexa may already respond to those by default. Two or three short words work well, and you can add a **weekday time schedule** (often labeled "At a scheduled time" or "Schedule") so the same routine also runs automatically Monday through Friday.

💬 Example: voice trigger phrase
**Start my morning**

If the app doesn't show a "phrase" trigger option, look for a "Custom" trigger or an "Alexa+" tag — newer versions sometimes bury voice phrases behind a different label.

**You'll know it worked when** the app shows your trigger phrase written down, and the routine is now ready to accept actions.

## Step 4 — Stack the actions in the order you want them to run
This is the main build. Look for a button like **Add action** inside the routine editor, then go through your written list one item at a time. Each action is its own little step — Alexa plays one, finishes, then moves to the next, in the order you add them.

Common actions to stack: **News** (pick a provider — a national broadcaster or a flash briefing), **Weather** (Alexa uses your device's home location by default), **Calendar** (read today's events — only works if you've already linked Google, Outlook or Apple Calendar inside the Alexa app's settings), and **Smart Home → Lights** (pick a named device like "Bedroom Lamp" and set the action to "Power on").

Keep the total under about ten actions for now. Long routines can hit the app's per-routine limit, and a five-minute morning briefing is usually plenty.

💬 Example: action stack (copyable names for the "Add action" prompts)
**1.** News → Flash briefing → [your preferred provider]
**2.** Weather → Today's forecast
**3.** Calendar → Read today's events
**4.** Smart Home → Lights → Bedroom Lamp → Power on

**You'll know it worked when** the action list shows your items in the exact order you added them, with no missing pieces.

## Step 5 — Save the routine and test it hands-free
Tap **Save** (or **Create**, depending on your app version) at the top or bottom of the routine editor. The routine now lives in your Alexa account and is ready to run.

Stand in the same room as your Alexa device and say your trigger phrase out loud — exactly as you typed it. Alexa should respond with the first action (usually the news briefing), wait for it to finish, then move to weather, then calendar, then the light. If you added a weekday time schedule in Step 3, the same routine will also start automatically at that time on Mondays through Fridays.

If something doesn't fire — for example, the calendar stays silent — go back to Step 4 and check that the calendar is actually linked in the Alexa app's settings. Routines can only call on features that are already connected.

💬 Example: spoken test command
**Alexa, start my morning.**

**You'll know it worked when** Alexa speaks the news, then the weather, then your events, then the lamp turns on — all from one spoken phrase.

## Common mistakes
- **Picking a trigger phrase that overlaps with a built-in Alexa command** (like "Alexa, good morning"). Alexa may run its default response instead of yours. **Fix:** choose a longer or more unique phrase, like "Start my morning" or "Begin weekday morning."
- **Skipping the calendar or smart-light setup before testing.** A routine can't call on a feature that isn't connected yet. **Fix:** go into the Alexa app's Settings → Calendars (or Smart Home) first, link the account and name the device, then come back to the routine.
- **Adding too many actions at once.** Long routines sometimes time out or hit a per-routine limit. **Fix:** aim for 5–8 actions and put detailed updates (a longer news briefing, a full calendar readout) earlier in the order so they finish first.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** a single spoken phrase replaces four taps on your phone, and the same routine fires every weekday morning without you remembering to launch anything.
- **For your business or work:** if you start your day from a home office, the same pattern — weather, calendar, news — doubles as a two-minute standup before you open your email.
- **If you want to go further:** add a conditional step (some Alexa+ versions let a routine branch on whether it's a workday or weekend), chain a second routine that starts a coffee maker or a focus playlist, or duplicate the routine and tweak a copy for evenings.

## Try it now
Open the Alexa app, find Routines, create one named "Weekday Morning", and add just two actions today: Weather and one smart light. Say your trigger phrase out loud. You'll see the workflow in five minutes — and tomorrow morning you can drop in the news and calendar steps in under two.
